title: What will you leave?
hook: a well, a book, a child's prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, two backpacks, trophies and stones, and the seerah's pardon at Mecca, and your line: carry it lightly. Did one old grievance loosen, even a little? Day one thousand fifty-nine.

A well, dug in hot ground, still giving water long after the man who paid for it is gone. A book, copied and recopied, still being read by people who will never meet its author. A child, grown up now, raising her hands after the prayer and asking mercy for a parent who died years ago. Three things. None of them is a building with a name on it, or a fortune, or a title. And yet a saying of the Prophet ﷺ names exactly these three as the things that keep working after a life ends. Today, a question with no deadline except one.
screen: `A WELL, STILL GIVING WATER.` → `A BOOK, STILL BEING READ.` → `A CHILD, STILL PRAYING.`

segments.voice: First, the saying itself. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: a charity that keeps on flowing, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. Three doors left open after the house is closed. Second, the flowing charity. Its Arabic name is sadaqa jariya, a charity that keeps on flowing. Abu Dawud keeps a story about a companion, Sa'd ibn Ubada, whose mother had died. He asked the Prophet which charity was best, and the answer was water. So Sa'd dug a well and said it was for his mother. A report in Tirmidhi also tells of a well in Medina that Uthman bought so people could draw from it freely. Water, given once, keeps giving. Third, the knowledge. This whole year has been full of it: scholars who wrote, teachers who taught a single student who taught another. A lesson passed on keeps working in someone else's life, whether or not anyone remembers who taught it first. Fourth, the child's prayer. The hadith's words are a righteous child who prays for the parent: a son or a daughter, after the prayer, asking mercy by name. Then notice what's missing from the list: wealth and power. A well can be a share in one. Knowledge can be one skill taught well. And the Qur'an widens the frame, in a verse that speaks of a record of what people sent ahead and the traces they left behind.
screen: `WHEN A PERSON DIES, THREE THINGS GO ON.` · `SADAQA JARIYA: CHARITY THAT RUNS LIKE WATER.` · `KNOWLEDGE THAT KEEPS ON WORKING.` · `A RIGHTEOUS CHILD WHO PRAYS FOR THEM.` · then, large: `WHAT THEY SENT AHEAD, AND THE TRACES THEY LEFT.`

segments.voice: The practice: plan one lasting good. Settle, and breathe. Look at the three doors. A well: is there something you could fund or join that keeps giving, water, a book for a library, a tree, a scholarship, a ramp? Knowledge: is there one thing you know that someone younger needs, a recipe, a skill, how to pray, how to fix a bike? A child's prayer: is there a child in your life you could be more present for? Choose one door. Then make it small enough to start this week. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it. If not, simply hold the plan. The bell holds the time.
Sadaqa jariya, a flowing charity like a well that keeps giving water long after the person who paid for it is gone. Today's word.
Your line: three doors left open. Today, take the first small step on the lasting good you chose: a message, a payment, a lesson offered, an hour set aside. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1059 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CHAIN BACK TO HIM.`

howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqa jariya in forms such as funding wells, mosques, schools, copies of the Qur'an or trees, often on behalf of parents who have died, and children make du'a for their parents after prayer.

fork.setup: you are Sa'd ibn Ubada. your mother has died, and you want to give charity for her. you ask the Prophet which charity is best. what does he say?
fork.reveal: he said water. Sa'd dug a well and said it was for his mother. in a hot land, water given once keeps giving.

original.note: Arabic: flowing charity, a good that keeps working after the giver has died.

trapdoor: what you thought: a legacy means a fortune or a famous name.
what it means: three things go on after death: flowing charity, useful knowledge, a child's prayer.
what a scholar hears: the hadith counts three, and Qur'an 36:12 speaks of a record of what people sent ahead and the traces they left.
recall: the bond that holds a group together

notes: Muslim 1631 (three things continue after death): paraphrased; confirm number.
Abu Dawud 1681, Sa'd ibn Ubada's well for Umm Sa'd: confirm number and grading.
Tirmidhi 3703, Uthman and the well of Rumah: confirm number and grading; told as 'a report'.
Qur'an 36:12 paraphrased ('what they sent ahead and the traces they left'); Pickthall's exact wording not quoted.
Trapdoor: jariya as 'running/flowing' (from jarā, to flow, as of water). Keeper to confirm this is acceptable under the etymology rule; it is the standard sense of the phrase.
Practice lists modern examples (tree, scholarship, ramp) as possible forms of lasting charity; Keeper may adjust.

Audit (serious): the teach, a screen head and a myth reveal extended the hadith's 'righteous child' (walad salih) to 'any child you helped raise, teach or love' and ruled that a silent du'a 'counts'; both are rulings the hadith does not give. Rewritten to the hadith's own terms (a son or daughter who prays for the parent). Whether prayers of others reach the dead is a separate fiqh question for a Keeper. The 36:12 line moved to close the teach instead of sitting inside the child's-prayer point; 'many Muslims' cut from howItsDone. The practice's 'a child you could be more present for' is left as an invitation, not as the hadith's third door; Keeper may adjust.
